query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐component concentrated alloys, the degree of local chemical order (LCO) governs their strength and failure behavior by generating spatial fluctuations in stacking fault energies and lattice strains that impede dislocation motion. In other words, samples with enhanced LCO form a rugged energy landscape that raises the activation barriers for dislocation glide, leading to higher yield strength and altered deformation (e.g., heterogeneous dislocation patterns), while samples with near‐ideal random solid-solution structures deform by conventional dislocation slip.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase concentrated alloy (for example, an FCC NiCoCr high-/medium‐entropy alloy or a similar multi‐component system) initially processed to have minimal LCO (i.e. close to a random solid solution).
generation.intervention: Control the degree of LCO via processing – for instance, by annealing at different temperatures: one set of samples is annealed at lower temperatures (or using processing routes that favor LCO development) and a baseline set is processed to maintain a random solid solution.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under quasi‐static tensile loading (or controlled compression) at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures with comparable strain rates (e.g., ~10^−3 s^−1) and similar grain sizes.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering which leads to heterogeneous local lattice distortions and spatial fluctuations in generalized stacking fault energies.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced LCO creates regions with locally higher fault energies, thereby impeding dislocation glide. This causes dislocations to adopt roughened or nonuniform slip paths that delay plastic flow and enhance yield strength. In contrast, a more random alloy state offers a smoother energy landscape for dislocation motion, resulting in lower strength and more uniform slip.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a random solid solution baseline, samples with higher LCO will exhibit a moderately higher yield strength (e.g., on the order of 10–20% increase) and show more heterogeneous dislocation patterns and altered strain-hardening behavior during deformation.
generation.baseline: A nearly ideal random solid solution processed to minimize LCO (e.g., via high-temperature homogenization and rapid quenching).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant in alloys where atomic size mismatches and strong enthalpic interactions favor chemical ordering; it may be less dominant in systems where other strengthening mechanisms (like precipitation strengthening) prevail or in alloy systems with negligible lattice distortion.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds upon observations of LCO variability affecting dislocation dynamics (as reported in PMC6687833 in both the introduction and variable LCO sections) and on evidence of heterogeneous strengthening linked to local fluctuations in fault energies (PMC9231497). Extending these LCO effects from model FCC/MEA systems to other alloy systems (e.g., BCC refractory HEAs where edge dislocation behavior is noted) introduces uncertainty regarding universality.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the same multi-component alloy (e.g., NiCoCr) with identical chemical compositions but processed to yield distinctly different degrees of LCO. Confirm the LCO levels via atomic-scale imaging or chemical short-range order parameter measurements. Perform controlled tensile tests and in situ TEM to monitor dislocation behavior and measure yield strength and strain hardening.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress from stress–strain curves
Dislocation structure and slip pattern via in situ TEM imaging
Quantitative assessment of LCO (e.g., using pairwise short-range order parameters)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens with enhanced LCO do not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength or exhibit similar dislocation behavior as the random solid solution samples (i.e., no detectable change in energy barriers for dislocation motion), then the hypothesis that LCO-induced energy landscape fluctuations govern the alloy’s strength and deformation mechanisms would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In what follows we systematically demonstrate, using an atomistic model that mimics the FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA), the new features rendered by the concentrated compositions: complex stacking fault (CSF) energy (CSFE) that is varying spatially and with processing conditions, local antiphase boundary (APB) energy, unconventional twin boundary energy and martensite phase boundary energy, and elevated lattice resistance to dislocation motion because of the rugged energy landscape. We show that the presence of multi-principal elements and their variable LCO make dislocations behave differently from conventional metals and dilute solutions, in terms of slip paths and activated nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) processes that govern alloy strength. The multitude of (partial) dislocation behavior associated with the adjustable LCOs opens new opportunities to tailor properties, through judicious choice of processing parameters, in particular, the homogenization annealing temperature (Ta).

cited_evidence.text: We first demonstrate the vast range of LCO in a concentrated SS of a given composition. We chose the FCC MEA NiCoCr as a model because it is a representative of multi-principal element systems and its mechanical properties are typical of (and often better than) other quaternary and quinary HEAs,. To enable insightful large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which are sorely needed to provide atomistic insight about dislocation behavior and adequate statistics, but have thus far been lacking in the HEA field, we developed an empirical interatomic potential for NiCoCr alloys without consideration of spin polarization (Methods). This model is designed to capture the typical features of HEAs: multi-principal constituents (equiatomic composition) with similar atomic sizes, chemical interactions consistent with typical MEA solutions, and single-phase solution but with variable LCO. A comprehensive discussion of this new potential is presented in Supplementary Note 1 (see Supplementary Figs. 1–7 and Supplementary Tables 1–2 for property validations). SignificanceMulti–principal element alloys exhibit outstanding mechanical properties owing to severe atomic lattice distortion. However, the heterogeneous strain caused by lattice distortion at the microscopic or mesoscopic scale has been ignored for a long time because the heterogeneous strain field is difficult to quantify and characterize. Our experiments and simulations clearly show that the heterogeneous strain field can contribute to the enhanced mechanical properties of multi–principal element alloys through the new heterogeneous strain-induced strengthening mechanisms, leading to the strength-ductility synergy in severely distorted compositionally complex crystals. Multi–principal element alloys (MPEAs) exhibit outstanding mechanical properties because the core effect of severe atomic lattice distortion is distinctly different from that of traditional alloys. However, at the mesoscopic scale the underlying physics for the abundant dislocation activities responsible for strength-ductility synergy has not been uncovered.
